turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_process_train.csv: 300 real samples, columns
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S, Heat treatment step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1 time, Heat treatment step 1
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2 temperature, Heat treatment step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 3 temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time, Heat treatment step 3
    cooling rate, Secondary treatment step 1 temperature, Secondary treatment step 1 time, Secondary treatment step 2
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 2 time, Secondary treatment step 3 temperature, Secondary treatment step 3
    time, Secondary treatment step 4 temperature, Secondary treatment step 4 time, Thermal exposure
    temperature, Thermal exposure time) and `target` (the measured yield strength
    at room temperature (MPa)).
  - b3_htsteel_process_pool.csv: 34 CANDIDATE samples whose yield strength
    at room temperature (MPa) was NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and
    the same process/composition columns.

Using the training data, predict which candidates have the HIGHEST yield
strength at room temperature (MPa), then select the 5 best candidates from
the pool.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit ranked
list of candidate_ids, best first, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904,
c905".
turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning

**All 34 candidates are essentially the same family:** ~13 wt% Cr, ~0.2 C martensitic stainless steels (three closely related compositions), austenitized at 1000–1050 °C. The only strongly varying process variable is the **Heat treatment step 2 temperature** (the tempering step, 200–740 °C), plus an optional aging step.

**What the training data says about this family**

Looking at 13Cr / 11Cr martensitic rows, yield strength is dominated by tempering temperature (Heat treatment step 2), not by the small compositional differences:

| Alloy (≈13Cr martensitic) | Heat treatment step 2 T (°C) | target |
|---|---|---|
| 83.73 / 11.25Cr | 200 | 1330 |
| 5.25Cr | 200 | 990 |
| 83.73 / 11.25Cr | 400 | 1340 |
| 82.95 / 11.25Cr | 475 | 1430 |
| 83.85 (13Cr, 0.4C) | 500 | 1390 |
| 82.95 | 500 | 1190 |
| 84.13 (13Cr) | 540 | 780 |
| 84.75 (13Cr, 0.4C) | 550 | 885–960 |
| 5.25Cr | 550 | 760 |
| 84.45 / 85.33 (13Cr, 0.3C) | 625–650 | 700–720 |
| 84.63 / 84.17 (13Cr, 0.12C) | 745–750 | 430–580 |
| 84.13 (13Cr) + 500 °C aging | 750 | 370 |

So the trend is monotone and very strong: **temper ≤ 500 °C → 1100–1400 MPa; 550–650 °C → 700–1000 MPa; 715–750 °C → 350–600 MPa.** Additional long aging at 500–600 °C further softens these steels (over-tempering).

**Applying this to the pool**

- Low-temper candidates (no aging): c015 (200 °C), c021 (200 °C), c017 (300 °C), c018 (300 °C), c006 (450 °C), c014 (450 °C), c004 (500 °C), c031 (500 °C) → predicted highest (≈1100–1400 MPa).
- Mid: c016, c027 (600 °C) → ~800–900 MPa.
- All remaining candidates temper at 715–740 °C, many with extra 500–600 °C aging → predicted 350–600 MPa (worst).

Composition differences among the three variants (0.2 C ± Ti/Cu, 0.6 Ni) are minor and second-order compared to the tempering temperature, so ranking is set by temper temperature (lowest first), with the slightly richer Ti/Cu/Mn/Si variant favored on ties for extra solid-solution/precipitation strengthening.

**Predicted ranking:** the two 200 °C tempers first, then the two 300 °C tempers, then the 450 °C temper.

Final: c015, c021, c017, c018, c006
